title: First weeks in New York in 1944: the Onyx, 52nd Street and a big city
summary: Jones describes arriving in New York, hearing Tatum, Gillespie, Hawkins, Byas and Monk, sightseeing, and deciding never to live in Chicago again.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: When you were on the 20th Century Limited, you were going to Chicago with the Stuff Smith Trio, and John Levy lost his ticket, and you said this was your first trip, you and John, this was the first time you'd been to
New York City.
Yes.
Then what happened? You said there was crowd waiting to meet you at the station?
No, at the Onyx Club, that opening night.
Oh.

Oh, I have something funny to tell you about that. As soon as we got to New York and got established where we were going to stay, or live, and in those days New York was so beautiful, I knew then I was never going to go back to Chicago. Just to see my people and my father and whatever, but I wasn't about to go back to the midwest, because there was a warmness about New York, and an excitement. Your blood started circulating. That's the only way I can describe it, you know. And John and I, we just -- we had a good time going through all the clubs. We had a couple of days before we were to open, and there was Art Tatum with his trio, with Slam Stewart and Tiny Grimes, and there was Dizzy Gillespie across the street, and Erroll Garner wasn't too far away from us. And Coleman Hawkins and Don Byas, playing together, which was quite a tenor treat. And Thelonius Monk was playing piano. And we just didn't see this in Chicago, you know. We saw -- even though the clubs in New York were just made over cellars or whatever you might want to call them, but there was that atmosphere, the sophistication.
What year was this, when you got to New York?
1944. And John kids me. He tries -- he says, "You know, Jimmy, you're getting old." Now it's 35 years ago. And I just tell him, I say, "Look, no matter how old I get I will never be as old as you."
(Laughter)

That's the only answer, and that's the only thing that slows him up, you know. So I can almost remember every moment of it. Then we -- John and I used to get on the subway. We thought we were sightseeing, but how can you see anything underground? And we would go uptown in the Bronx and go way downtown and look at the Statue of Liberty, and all these things that we'd seen by postcard.
Uh-huh.

And then looking at the Empire State Building. Boy, that was like Alice in Wonderland. And the enthusiasm of youth at that time, you know? Because I used to listen to the Glenn Miller Orchestra, the Army orchestra he had before he went overseas, you know, and I liked Glenn Miller's work, and I was allowed to go into the NBC Radio Center, you know, and look at the scores and everything. You know, I was just -- they just let me in. And I was so surprised to see -- that's one thing about New York, you would see the biggest of people right next door to you. You know, you wouldn't see it in other

cities. And I'd run into guys like Paul Whiteman in the elevator, and you know, people that you just knew of. And they talked with you, you know, and said, 'Wait, look, I'm going across the street and have a beer and a corned beef sandwich. Want to join me?' And I'm sitting there looking ga-ga, you know?
(Laughter)

It's funny. Then after awhile I began to get tied into the lifestyle of that community, and when I went back to Chicago, gee whiz, it looked like a farm town, even though it's still a big, major city. But it just -- well, it was nothing like New York.
Didn't have that spirit.
No. It was nothing like New York. And I believe that New York is still the same. I haven't been back there for years.
I think it is.
Yeah, I think it's still the same. It just had to go through its financial transitions, but the culture is still there, I believe.
And the spirit of the people.
Yeah. It's a boss city, you know.
Uh-huh.
